title: Book store - Serverless Book store Intro - Writing first functions
content:
Book store - Serverless Book store Intro - Writing first functions Overview This is a series about Serverless. AWS provides technologies for running code, managing data, and integrating applications, all without managing servers. Those technologies serve users to create applications under the Serverless model. Serverless applications start with AWS Lambda, save data with DynamoDB, receive user requests with API Gateway, host static web with S3/AWS Amplify Console, …
Example of a web application using the Serverless model with the cloud:
In the first post of this series, we’ll learn the basics of Serverless and practice creating functions with Lambda that are triggered from S3 and write data to a DynamoDB table.
Content Introduction Create Lambda function to resize images Create Lambda function to write data to DynamoDB

title: Create DynamoDB table
content:
Open DynamoDB console, then Click Create table. Enter table name: Books.
Enter partition key: id. Scroll down to Table settings pattern, select Customize settings.
In Table class pattern, select DynamoDB Standard. In Read/write capacity setting pattern, select On-demand. Scroll down, leave as default and click Create table.

title: Create resize image Lambda function
content:
Open AWS Lambda console, then click Create function button. At Create function page.
Choose Author from scratch. Enter function name, such as resize-image. Choose Node.js 20.x for Runtime. Leave as default and click Create function button. Download source code file to your device Source codefunction.zip(25968 ko)At resize-image page.
Click Upload from button. Choose .zip file. At Upload a .zip file modal.
Click Upload button and select the downloaded source code file. Click Save. At resize-image page.
Click Configuration tab. Click Environment variables on the left menu. Click Edit. At Edit environment variables page.
Click Add environment variable, then add the following environment variables: WIDTH: enter the new width of the photo, such as 200px. HEIGHT: enter the new hight of the photo, such as 280px. DES_BUCKET: S3 bucket name to store the changed image, such as: book-image-resize-stores-by-myself. Then click Save. So we have completed the step of creating a Lambda function and configuring the environment variables for it. Next step, we will create an S3 bucket to store uploaded and edited images.

title: Introduction
content:
Overview Before starting to write the first Lambda function, let’s learn through the concept of Serverless, and Lambda.
Serverless Serverless is a basic concept that refers to a group of services that are fully managed by AWS. When using these services, you will not need to care about basic daily infrastructure administration tasks such as updating security patches, managing device portfolios, managing assets….
There are many services planned into the Serverless cluster on AWS such as serverless databases like Aurora Serverless, Redshift Serverless, serverless compute like AWS Lambda.
AWS Lambda Lambda is a serverless compute service that allows you to run applications without initializing or managing servers. Lambda runs on a highly available infrastructure platform and does all of the compute resource management, including server and operating system maintenance, capacity provisioning, auto-scaling, and logging. . With Lambda, you can develop almost any kind of backend application or service.
You organize your application into Lambda functions. Lambda functions run only when needed and are capable of automatically scaling, from a few requests per day to thousands per second. You only pay for the compute time you use — AWS won’t charge when your application is not running.
We’ll also start our Serverless Journey with a Lambda function that first resizes the image after uploading it to the S3 bucket, saves the edited image to a new S3 bucket, and deletes the old image.

title: Create S3 bucket
content:
In this part, we will create two S3 buckets:
Bucket book-image-stores-by-myself: to store uploaded image. Bucket book-image-resize-stores-by-myself: to store image after resize. Open Amazon S3 console, then click Create bucket. At Create bucket page.
Choose Bucket type: General purpose. Enter bucket name, book-image-stores-by-myself. Choose ACLs disabled. Uncheck access block: Block all public access. Check the box: I acknowledge that the current settings might result in this bucket and the objects within becoming public. Click Create bucket. To create bucket - book-image-resize-stores-by-myself, repeat steps 1 to 5.
At resize-image page. We add the trigger.
Click Add Trigger. Enter S3 and select S3 service. At At trigger page.
Select bucket book-image-stores-by-myself that trigger lambda. Select All object create events for Event type. Check the box - I acknowledge that using…. as shown below. Click Add. Check result after add trigger for Lambda function.

title: Write data by Lambda function
content:
In this step, we create Lambda function to write data to created DynamoDB table.
Open AWS Lambda console.
Click Functions. Click Create function. At Create function page.
Choose Author from scratch. Enter function name: book_create. Select Python 3.11 for Runtime Click Create function. At book_create page.
Copy the below code into lambda_function tab.
import boto3import jsonclient = boto3.resource('dynamodb')def lambda_handler(event, context):book_item = event["body"]error = Nonetry:table = client.Table('Books')table.put_item(Item = book_item)except Exception as e:error = eif error is None:response = {'statusCode': 200,'body': 'writing to dynamoDB successfully!','headers': {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},}else:response = {'statusCode': 400,'body': 'writing to dynamoDB fail!','headers': {'Content-Type': 'application/json'},}return response Click Deploy. Next, add additional permissions for Lambda to access to DynamoDB.
Click to tab Configure. Click Permissions on the left menu. Click to the function executing role. Click Attach permissions. Select Attach policies. Enter AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess to search policy. Choose AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess policy. Click Add permission. Create an event to test the function operation. At book_create page.
Click to tab Test. Enter event name, such as: test_1. Enter the below data into Event JSON. {"body": {"id": "1","name": "Java","author": "Alex","category": "IT","price": "10.89","description": "This book guide to create Java web basic","image": "https://book-image-resize-store.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/Java.jpg"}} Click Save. Click Test. Navigate to DynamoDB Tables console.
Choose Books Tables. Click Actions. Click Update settings Click Explore table items. You will get all the data from the table.

title: Create Policy for Lambda function
content:
In this part, we will create a Policy that grants the Lambda function permission to get, write, and delete objects in the S3 bucket.
At resize-image page.
Click tab Configuration. Click Permissions. Click on the role being executed by the function. At resize-image-role-… page.
Click Add permissions. Select Create inline policy. At Step 1: Specify permissions page.
Click Choose a service and Enter S3. Select S3. Enter GetObject at Search box. Choose GetObject at Read level. Clear Search box and enter DeleteObject. Choose DeleteObject at Write level. Click Add ARNs. At Specify ARNs modal. Enter book-image-stores-by-myself at Resource bucket name. Enter * at Resource object name. Click Add ARNs button. Click + Add more permissions. Click Choose a service and Enter S3. Select S3. Enter PutObject. Choose PutObject at Write level. Click Add ARNs. At Specify ARNs modal. Enter book-image-resize-stores-by-myself at Resource bucket name. Enter * at Resource object name. Click Add ARNs button. After modal is closed, click Next. At Step 2: Review and create page.
Enter policy name, such as: LambdaResizeImageS3Policy. Review policy information and click Create policy. Check policies just created. We have finished granting the Lambda function read, write, and delete permissions from the S3 bucket. The next step is to test the Lambda function working when uploading an image.

title: Clean up
content:
Delete DynamoDB table.
Open DynamoDB console. Select Tables on the left menu. Select Books table. Click Delete. Enter confirm and click Delete table. Delete S3 bucket.
Open S3 console. Select book-image-resize-stores-by-myself bucket. Click Empty. Enter permanently delete and click Empty. Select book-image-resize-stores-by-myself bucket. Click Delete. Enter book-image-resize-stores-by-myself and click Delete bucket. Select book-image-stores-by-myself bucket. Click Delete. Enter book-image-stores-by-myself and click Delete bucket. Delete Lambda function.
Open AWS Lambda console. Select book_create function. Click Actions. Select Delete. Enter delete and click Delete. Similar to resize_image function. If you continue with workshop 2 of the series, you can skip the step of deleting the Lambda function.

title: Test Lambda function operation
content:
Navigate to S3 bucket: book-image-stores-by-myself.
Click Upload. At Upload page.
Click Add files. Choose files and click Upload. Wait for the Lambda function running, then check whether the image has been deleted. Navigate to S3 bucket: book-image-resize-stores-by-myself.
Click to image file. Click Object URL to download image. But error occurs - Access Denied. To download image, need add policy for bucket to allow public access.
Back to bucket, select Permission. Click Edit in Bucket policy. Copy the below json data into Policy. {"Version": "2012-10-17","Statement": [{"Sid": "PublicReadGetObject","Effect": "Allow","Principal": "*","Action": "s3:GetObject","Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::book-image-resize-stores-by-myself/*"}]} Click Save changes. Then, repeat steps 4 and 5 to download image to local to download an image to your device to compare it with the one you’ve already uploaded. So Lambda resizes function is working properly.
